steps.body: Algebra 1's discriminant chart had a hole: 'D < 0: no real solutions.' The full story: **every** quadratic has exactly **two** roots. D > 0: two distinct reals. D = 0: one real, counted twice. D < 0: two complex conjugates. Nothing is ever missing — it just moves off the real line.

widget.prompt: For x² + x + 1 = 0, D = 1 − 4 = −3. What does that mean now?

options.label: two complex conjugate roots
options.feedback: Right — the roots exist; they're just off the real line, as a conjugate pair.

options.label: no solutions at all
options.feedback: That was the Algebra 1 shorthand — the equation HAS two solutions; they're complex.

options.label: two distinct real roots
options.feedback: D < 0 means the parabola misses the x-axis — the roots are complex, not real.

options.label: one repeated root
options.feedback: One repeated root is the D = 0 boundary case — D = −3 gives a complex PAIR.

steps.body: So classifying is a one-number job: compute D = b² − 4ac and read its **sign**. Positive → two real crossings. Zero → the vertex kisses the axis. Negative → the parabola floats clear and the pair goes complex.

explanationVariants: b² = 9 and 4ac = 32; subtracting gives −23 — complex pair.

commonErrors.feedback: 9 − 32 is NEGATIVE: −23 — this one's roots are a complex pair.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 9 − 32 = −23; negative, so two complex conjugate roots.

widget.prompt: Drag each equation to its root type (use the sign of D = b² − 4ac).

items.label: x² − 9 = 0
items.feedback: D = 0 + 36 = 36 > 0 — it crosses the axis twice, at ±3.

items.label: x² − 5x + 6 = 0
items.feedback: D = 25 − 24 = 1 > 0 — two distinct real roots (2 and 3).

items.label: x² + 6x + 9 = 0
items.feedback: D = 36 − 36 = 0 — the perfect square (x + 3)² kisses the axis once.

items.label: x² + 4 = 0
items.feedback: D = 0 − 16 = −16 < 0 — the pair ±2i, off the real line.

widget.missFeedback: Compute D for each: positive means two real, zero means repeated, negative means complex pair.
widget.successFeedback: All six sorted — the sign of D alone settles every case.

explanationVariants: Repeated root needs D = 36 − 4c = 0, so c = 9 — and indeed x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)².
Set the discriminant to zero and solve for c: 4c = 36.

widget.prompt: For what value of c does x² + 6x + c = 0 have exactly one repeated root?

options.label: c = 9
options.feedback: Right — D = 36 − 4c = 0 at c = 9, the perfect square (x + 3)².

options.label: c = 6
options.feedback: That copies b — the condition is 36 − 4c = 0, so c = 9.

options.label: c = 36
options.feedback: 36 is b² — but D = b² − 4c, so 4c must equal 36: c = 9.

options.label: c = −9
options.feedback: c = −9 makes D = 36 + 36 > 0 — two REAL roots, not a repeat.

explanationVariants: D = b² − 64 = 0 needs b² = 64: b = 8 works (b = −8 would too).

widget.prompt: Which value of b gives x² + bx + 16 = 0 exactly one repeated root?

options.label: b = 4
options.feedback: D = 16 − 64 = −48 < 0 — that sends the roots complex, not repeated.

options.label: b = 16
options.feedback: D = 256 − 64 = 192 > 0 — two distinct real roots. The balance point is b² = 64.

options.label: b = 2
options.feedback: D = 4 − 64 = −60 < 0 — a complex pair. You need b² = 64.

explanationVariants: D = 100 − 4c = 0 gives c = 25 — the perfect square (x − 5)².
Half of −10 is −5, and (−5)² = 25: completing the square and the discriminant agree.

widget.prompt: For what value of c does x² − 10x + c = 0 have exactly one repeated root?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 is b² — the repeated-root condition is b² = 4c, so c = 100/4 = 25.
5 is b/2 — the constant of the perfect square is (b/2)² = 25.

steps.body: Every quadratic has exactly two roots — D's sign says where they live.
takeaways: D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: one repeated; D < 0: a conjugate pair.
'No real solutions' really means 'both solutions went complex'.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: sum and product of roots survive the trip into the complex plane.

concept.body: D = b² − 4ac with every sign intact. For x² + 1 = 0: a = 1, b = 0, c = 1.

explanationVariants: D = 0 − 4 = −4 — negative, so the roots (±i) are a complex pair.

widget.prompt: For x² + 1 = 0, what is the discriminant?

commonErrors.feedback: The 4ac term subtracts: 0 − 4 = −4 — that minus is what makes the roots ±i.
b = 0, but D isn't b² alone: D = 0 − 4(1)(1) = −4.
